title: Shannon feasibility from algorithmic network coding
formal: For every fixed finite acyclic directed network with correlated finite-alphabet sources and specified source-reconstruction demands, does high-probability algorithmic feasibility on independent source blocks imply Shannon achievability at the same edge rates? The algorithmic model permits sample-dependent local programs of length \(O(\log N)\) and \(O(\log N)\) extra bits on each edge for a block of \(N\) samples. The Shannon model requires fixed local encoding and decoding maps for each block length, with vanishing error and arbitrarily small rate slack, as defined below.
why: The question compares information transmission for random sources with transmission of their individual realized strings. A positive answer would show that logarithmic sample-dependent algorithmic descriptions cannot create new asymptotic network rates. A negative answer would expose a concrete operational distinction between Shannon and Kolmogorov descriptions of distributed information.
status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. Question 13 explicitly leaves the converse unresolved in the 2021 source, reposted in 2022. The 2006 source grounds the algorithmic model but does not settle the general comparison. No matching proof or counterexample was found in the bounded later-work search; current openness is not exhaustively certified.

progress.text: Shen states the acyclic algorithmic-network model with logarithmic local complexity allowances and relates several classical information-theoretic examples to it.
The problem list explicitly asks whether high-probability algorithmic feasibility for independent joint-source samples can exceed Shannon feasibility.
The authors deposit the problem list on arXiv; this is a later source version, not a new coding theorem.

sentences: Several correlated sources must be transmitted through a fixed directed acyclic network to designated recipients.
Shannon coding chooses local encoding and decoding maps that work with high probability for random source blocks.
Algorithmic coding instead allows each realized block to have its own short local programs and compatible edge messages.
The question asks whether high-probability algorithmic feasibility with logarithmic overhead always implies Shannon feasibility at the same asymptotic rates.
The target is this general converse, with vanishing error and rate slack defined explicitly, rather than a finite-block equivalence inferred from the title.

definitions: Fix a finite directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,E)\), an integer \(m\ge1\), nonempty finite alphabets \(\mathcal X_1,\ldots,\mathcal X_m\), and any joint probability law \(P\) for \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_m)\) on their product. The law is fixed as block length varies; its coordinates may be arbitrarily correlated, and no computability assumption is imposed on its probabilities. Each vertex \(v\) has fixed sets \(S_v,T_v\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\): it initially receives the source coordinates in \(S_v\) and must reproduce the coordinates in \(T_v\). Require \(\bigcup_v S_v=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Several vertices may know or demand the same source, and a vertex may both receive sources and relay messages. Each edge \(e\) has a fixed finite real rate \(r_e\ge0\), measured in bits per joint source sample. For \(N\ge1\), take \(N\) independent copies of the entire vector \(X\); write \(X_j^N\) for the resulting length-\(N\) word of coordinate \(j\). The block law is \(P^{\otimes N}\), not independence between different coordinates. All finite words, integers and tuples use fixed computable binary encodings; tuple components and incident edges are ordered once with the network. Let \(C(u\mid v)\) be plain conditional Kolmogorov complexity: the least length of a binary program for a fixed optimal interpreter that halts with output \(u\) on auxiliary input \(v\). There is no time bound. Optimal means that this interpreter simulates every other partial computable interpreter with an additive program-length overhead independent of \(u,v\). Let \(L_N=\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). For a realized source block and an integer \(K\ge1\), algorithmic feasibility means that there exist edge-message strings \(M_e\) with \(|M_e|\le\lfloor Nr_e\rfloor+K L_N\), such that at every vertex \(v\), \[C\bigl(( (M_e)_{e\in\operatorname{out}(v)}, (X_j^N)_{j\in T_v})\mid N,(X_j^N)_{j\in S_v},(M_e)_{e\in\operatorname{in}(v)}\bigr)\le K L_N.\] The demanded outputs in this formula are the true source words, so reconstruction is exact on a feasible realization. Messages and witnessing programs may depend on the whole realized source block; only their lengths and the displayed local conditional complexities are constrained. They need not arise from one choice of encoding functions used for every realization. Call the rate vector algorithmically feasible with high probability if there exists one \(K\) such that, for every \(\eta\in(0,1)\), some \(N_0\) makes the probability of this feasibility event at least \(1-\eta\) for all \(N\ge N_0\). The same \(K\) works for every block length, realization and error threshold. Shannon achievability means that for every rate slack \(\delta>0\) and every error tolerance \(\eta\in(0,1)\), there is \(N_0\) such that for every \(N\ge N_0\) there exist deterministic local encoding and decoding maps with the following properties. In a topological order, each vertex computes its outgoing edge messages from only its local source words and incoming messages; each demand is decoded from the same local information. Each edge message belongs to the finite set of binary strings of length at most \(\lfloor N(r_e+\delta)\rfloor\). For each edge this bounded-string alphabet is shared by the parties and the receiver observes the whole message, including its length; the same convention is used for algorithmic messages. The probability, under \(P^{\otimes N}\), that every demanded word is reconstructed correctly is at least \(1-\eta\). The local maps are fixed before observing the source realization; they may depend on the network, law, rates, block length and tolerances, and have no computational time or description-size bound. There is no feedback, extra channel, shared sample-dependent advice or communication other than the edge messages. This is an asymptotic rate-region converse. It does not assert equivalence with logarithmic finite-block overhead in the Shannon model.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication for every network, source law, demand pattern and finite rate vector just defined, or refute it. A refutation requires a fixed admissible network, joint law and rate vector for which algorithmic feasibility holds with one logarithmic-overhead constant and probability tending to one, but Shannon achievability fails. In particular, failure at a single block length or at a rate boundary without accounting for arbitrarily small positive rate slack is insufficient. Results for only one source, independent sources, one terminal, particular network shapes, or only information-cut inequalities do not settle the general converse. An inefficient Shannon code is allowed; the target is coding feasibility, not efficient construction.

context_blocks.text: A network code chooses how each relay transforms its received messages and local source data. The same code must handle many possible source realizations. Several correlated sources and several destinations can make compatibility between these local choices a substantial constraint.

The algorithmic version instead asks whether a particular tuple of strings admits suitable edge messages. A short program may certify each local transformation, and a different realized tuple may use different programs. Their permitted logarithmic length is small compared with the transmitted source block, but this nonuniform freedom is exactly what the converse must address.

Shen’s 2006 framework defines algorithmic requests on finite acyclic directed graphs, with message-length capacities and logarithmic conditional-complexity allowances. The graph, local-information and program conventions in this card make that model explicit.

The 2021 problem list compares the two settings by taking independent repeated samples of a joint source law. Question 13 asks whether algorithmic feasibility with high probability can occur even when the corresponding Shannon transmission is impossible. The earlier direction from Shannon codes to algorithmic requests is discussed with an explicit warning that logarithmic precision may be lost.

Accordingly, the main target here is the converse actually asked in Question 13. It fixes logarithmic algorithmic overhead and the standard Shannon closure under vanishing error and positive rate slack. It does not claim a two-way finite-block equivalence, and it keeps arbitrary correlation within each source sample.

The source surveys networks where both theories have strong positive coding theorems, including transmission with side information and the two-sender Slepian–Wolf problem. It also discusses networks where elementary cut constraints do not suffice. Agreement in these special cases does not supply a general translation between the models.

The distinction is operational rather than a change of terminology for entropy. The conclusion requires one collection of local maps that succeeds on almost all realizations, while the premise only asserts the existence of compatible short local descriptions separately for those realizations.
